SNUSAT & APT — every released question, worked

The 120 questions Shiv Nadar University has published for the current pattern of its Scholastic Aptitude Test and Academic Proficiency Test, in the sample papers for 2025, 2026 and 2027 — each with the idea behind it, the working, and the mistake it is built to catch.

Each section then closes with ten predicted variations: new questions on the types the three papers keep returning to, tagged Predicted 2027. They are not SNU's, and their answers are worked here.

Answers are SNU's own key. Where the paper or its key is itself wrong, the slide says so in a red box and works the question properly: there are twelve such notes, so read them rather than assuming you have blundered.

Moving around

  • ← → or space to move, Home / End for the ends; swipe on a phone.
  • S shows or hides the solution, D marks a question done.
  • The menu in the bar jumps to a section; your place and your done-flags are remembered in this browser.
  • Printing lays out every slide with every solution open.

What you are sitting

SNUSAT is the entrance test for every undergraduate programme at the Delhi NCR campus. It is online and home-proctored, run in six cycles from January to July, and you may take it twice (a fresh application each time).

Applicants to B.Tech and BS Computer Science also sit the APT, which tests subject knowledge in Mathematics and Physics.

90 min		Logical Reasoning 2045 min

All questions are multiple choice and there is no negative marking — so never leave a blank. That is the single most valuable fact on this slide: with about two minutes a question in SNUSAT and ninety seconds in the APT, a considered guess costs nothing.

SNU's own documents disagree about what the two SNUSAT sections are called — the 2025 paper heads them Critical Thinking and Logical Reasoning, while its own table, and the whole of the 2026 paper, say Logical Reasoning and Quantitative Reasoning. The questions are the same either way, and this deck groups them by what they actually test.

What is examined

From SNU's admissions FAQ, which is the only syllabus the university publishes:

SectionSub-skills checked
Logical Reasoningreading comprehension · identifying logical fallacies · accurate conclusions and assumptions · matching examples to definitions · situation analysis and problem solving · argument and object classification
Quantitative Reasoningdata analysis · commercial math · visual reasoning · algebra · arithmetic · mensuration and volume · complex problem solving
APT Mathematicsalgebra and number theory · calculus · geometry and trigonometry · linear algebra and analytical geometry · probability · statistics and discrete mathematics
APT Physicselectricity and magnetism · light and optics · matter · motion and gravitation · thermodynamics · statics and dynamics

Two things the released papers make plain that the syllabus does not. The SNUSAT quantitative section is pitched at class 9–10 — ratio, percentage, mensuration, similar triangles — but wrapped in a diagram, a flowchart or a pattern you have to decode first. And the APT is squarely class 11–12, one idea per question, with very little heavy computation.

SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning

Reading an argument for what it actually commits itself to: assumptions, conclusions, fallacies, and two set-piece puzzles.

40 questions · 10 from the 2027 paper, 10 from 2026, 10 from 2025, then 10 predicted variations
1 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q11 mark done
Recognise it by: Match the definition, not the topic

In the context of Amartya Sen's ‘Capability Approach’, poverty is not just a matter of low income but also of “capability deprivation”, where individuals lack the freedoms and opportunities to achieve their full potential. Addressing poverty therefore requires ensuring access to resources, opportunities, and social participation. (Source: Amartya Sen, Development as Freedom, 1999)

Which of the following policy initiatives aligns BEST with Sen's Capability Approach to reducing poverty?

  1. Focusing on direct cash transfers to low-income families to alleviate immediate financial needs.
  2. Creating an inclusive safety net for equal access to services for marginalized communities.
  3. Encouraging private sector growth through deregulation and entrepreneurship incentives.
  4. Promoting urban migration to improve access to better job opportunities and services.

How to see it

The passage defines poverty as missing access and participation, not missing income. Pick the option that delivers access to all.

Working

  1. A treats poverty as low income — exactly what the passage says it is not just.
  2. C is a growth policy; it may raise incomes but promises nobody access.
  3. D asks the poor to move to opportunity rather than extending it to them, and is silent on marginalised groups.
  4. B gives equal access to services for the marginalised: resources, opportunities and participation, the three things the passage lists.
Answer — B — an inclusive safety net for equal access to services.
Common slip. Picking A because cash obviously helps. The question asks which fits Sen's definition best, not which helps at all.
2 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q12 mark done
Recognise it by: Main conclusion = the comparison the whole passage argues for

Many cities across India have responded to rising road accidents by imposing stricter traffic fines and vehicle penalties for speeding and rash driving. Traffic authorities argue that heavy penalties deter dangerous behaviour and reduce accident rates quickly. However, a study comparing cities in two states found that accident rates declined most in cities that invested in driver awareness campaigns, improved road design with better signage and safety features, and educated young riders through school-based road safety programmes — even when those cities spent less on enforcement and fines. Penalty-based approaches create anger among drivers, encourage bribery, and fail to address why people drive recklessly in the first place. Approaches such as driver education, community awareness campaigns, and safer road infrastructure address the root causes of accidents and build lasting safety habits.

Which of the following best states the author's main conclusion about reducing road accidents?

  1. Road design improvements and signage are the only factors that prevent accidents.
  2. Penalty-based enforcement alone does not effectively reduce road accidents long-term.
  3. Safer road infrastructure is necessary but driver education is not required for reducing accidents.
  4. Driver education, community awareness, and safer road infrastructure reduce accidents more effectively than strict penalties.

How to see it

The passage sets two approaches against each other and comes down on one side. The conclusion is that comparison, stated whole.

Working

  1. A says “only” one factor — the passage names three.
  2. C contradicts the passage, which praises driver education.
  3. B is true to the passage but is only half of it: it criticises penalties without saying what works better. It is a premise on the way.
  4. D carries both halves — what works, and that it works better than penalties.
Answer — D — education, awareness and safer roads beat strict penalties.
Common slip. Choosing B. It is supported, but a conclusion is the claim the evidence is marshalled for, and here that is the comparison.
3 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q13 mark done
Recognise it by: Transfer the principle, then find what it silently relies on

Many cities across India have responded to rising road accidents by imposing stricter traffic fines and vehicle penalties for speeding and rash driving. Traffic authorities argue that heavy penalties deter dangerous behaviour and reduce accident rates quickly. However, a study comparing cities in two states found that accident rates declined most in cities that invested in driver awareness campaigns, improved road design with better signage and safety features, and educated young riders through school-based road safety programmes — even when those cities spent less on enforcement and fines. Penalty-based approaches create anger among drivers, encourage bribery, and fail to address why people drive recklessly in the first place. Approaches such as driver education, community awareness campaigns, and safer road infrastructure address the root causes of accidents and build lasting safety habits.

Based on the principles demonstrated in the passage above, if a school applied this same approach to reduce classroom disruptions and student misbehaviour, which of the following would be a critical assumption for the plan's success?

  1. Classroom disruptions stem from lack of guidance and understanding rather than deliberate defiance.
  2. Strict punishment deters student misbehaviour more effectively than awareness and education programmes.
  3. Teachers will require extensive training before implementing awareness-based behaviour management systems.
  4. Teachers should blame parents entirely for not disciplining students at home adequately.

How to see it

The approach works by addressing root causes through education. That only helps if the root cause is something education can fix.

Working

  1. Negation test: if disruptions were deliberate defiance, guidance would not touch them, and the plan would fail. So A is essential.
  2. B is the opposite of the approach; assuming it would undermine the plan.
  3. C may be practically true, but the plan could succeed with modest training. It is not critical.
  4. D is blame-shifting, unrelated to the education-first principle.
Answer — A — disruptions stem from lack of guidance, not deliberate defiance.
Common slip. Picking C because it sounds like a sensible requirement. An assumption is something without which the argument collapses.
4 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q14 mark done
Recognise it by: Every part of the definition must appear in the example

FOMO stands for “Fear of Missing Out.” It describes the anxiety or worry that arises when you perceive that others are having rewarding, enjoyable, or important experiences that you are not part of. This feeling often leads to compulsive checking of social media, sudden changes in behaviour, or impulsive decisions made to avoid being left out. The key characteristic of FOMO is that the anxiety is driven by comparison with others' experiences and a fear of exclusion.

Which of the following situations best represents an example of FOMO?

  1. Aisha chose not to join the sports team because she preferred solo activities and hobbies.
  2. Priya felt disappointed because she couldn't afford a concert ticket that her friends attended.
  3. Rohan kept refreshing Instagram because his classmates posted about a party he wasn't invited to.
  4. Vikram spent three hours choosing what to wear to school because he wanted to look fashionable.

How to see it

Tick off the definition: others' experience, you excluded, anxiety, compulsive checking. Find the option with all four.

Working

  1. A is a free choice with no anxiety and no comparison.
  2. B has exclusion and comparison, but the feeling is disappointment about money, not anxious fear of missing out.
  3. D is about appearance, with no experience being missed.
  4. C: classmates' party (others' experience), not invited (exclusion), compulsive refreshing (the behaviour the definition names). Every element is present.
Answer — C — Rohan refreshing Instagram.
Common slip. Settling for B because friends are involved. It lacks the anxiety and the compulsive behaviour.
5 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q15 mark done
Recognise it by: One case → “everywhere”: a hasty generalisation

During a wildlife policy debate, a conservationist argues: “Region A created fully protected wetlands with no human activity. Since bird populations declined anyway, we should allow unrestricted community harvesting everywhere because protection clearly doesn't work.”

Which logical fallacy BEST describes the conservationist's reasoning?

  1. The conservationist blames all environmental damage entirely on community harvesting practices.
  2. The conservationist judges conservation effectiveness based only on Region A without examining why it failed.
  3. The conservationist assumes that unrestricted harvesting will improve bird populations more than any protection strategy.
  4. The conservationist treats Region A's failure as proof that all conservation protection strategies are ineffective.

How to see it

One region's result is stretched to a policy for everywhere. That is generalising from a sample of one — and it is made worse by not asking why the one failed.

Working

  1. A is the reverse of what was argued: the speaker wants more harvesting.
  2. C overstates: the speaker never claims harvesting improves bird numbers, only that protection does not work.
  3. B and D both describe the hasty generalisation. B stresses the thin evidence (one region, causes unexamined); D stresses the sweeping conclusion (all strategies).
  4. SNU's key gives B: the decline might have had causes unrelated to protection — disease, drought, upstream pollution — and the speaker never looked.
Answer — B — judging effectiveness on Region A alone without examining why it failed.
Common slip. Confusing the fallacy with its conclusion. Ask what is wrong with the reasoning, not what is wrong with the policy.
Careful — the paper itself. D is at least as good a description — it is the textbook wording of a hasty generalisation. SNU's key says B, and that is the answer marked here. If you meet this item in the exam, B is what scores; between two descriptions of the same fallacy, prefer the one about the evidence.
6 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q16 mark done
Recognise it by: Volunteers differ from non-volunteers — self-selection

A viral dance challenge on social media gained millions of views in one month. Teenagers who participated in the challenge posted videos of themselves dancing. Surveys conducted after the challenge showed that participating teens reported 25% higher confidence levels compared to non-participants. A social media influencer analysed this data and announced: “This dance challenge is a breakthrough for youth mental health. It directly boosted teenage confidence.”

Which statement best describes the logical error in the influencer's reasoning?

  1. The influencer concludes the challenge boosted confidence without considering that self-selected participants may already have higher confidence levels.
  2. The influencer judges confidence using only self-reported survey responses without supporting evidence from other sources.
  3. The influencer assumes that what worked for this one viral challenge would boost confidence in most other social media challenges too.
  4. The influencer ignores that social validation, not the physical act of dancing, might be the more likely explanation for the boost.

How to see it

Who posts videos of themselves dancing to millions? People who were confident already. A correlation between joining and confidence says nothing about which came first.

Working

  1. The data compare participants with non-participants after the event, with no “before” measurement. So the gap could have existed all along.
  2. And participation was voluntary: confident teens are exactly the ones likely to post a public dance video. That is self-selection, A.
  3. C is not what the influencer said (they spoke of this challenge only). B is a weakness of evidence, not the logical error in the causal claim.
  4. D proposes a different cause through the challenge — it still accepts that the challenge raised confidence, which is the very step that is unproven.
Answer — A (self-selection) by the reasoning; the key says D.
Common slip. Picking the option that names an alternative explanation for the boost when the problem is that no boost has been shown.
Careful — the paper itself. SNU's key gives D. D is a rival mechanism, but it concedes the causal claim the influencer has not earned. The error the data actually invite is reversed or pre-existing causation through self-selection, which is A. Both are marked; in the exam, the key scores.
7 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q17 mark done
Recognise it by: No True Scotsman = redefining the group to exclude a counterexample

Aryan has been an anime fan for three years. He watches anime regularly, discusses plot theories with friends, reads manga, and organises watch parties for new releases. Recently, he watched a popular anime in its dubbed version.

A No True Scotsman fallacy occurs when someone changes the definition of a group whenever someone doesn't fit the ideal, dismissing them and treating them as inauthentic members of that group.

Which of the following statements BEST represents a No True Scotsman fallacy in response to Aryan's anime fandom?

  1. “Real anime fans only watch subtitled versions. Since Aryan watched a dubbed version, he's not actually a true anime fan.”
  2. “Dubbed anime has lower quality voice acting than subtitled versions, so watching dubbed versions diminishes the viewing experience.”
  3. “Aryan watched a dubbed anime, but dubbing still requires significant production effort and resources.”
  4. “If Aryan watches one dubbed anime, he'll eventually stop watching subtitled versions completely.”

How to see it

Look for the words “real” or “true” attached to a new, convenient condition for membership.

Working

  1. A adds a never-before-stated rule (“real fans only watch subtitles”) precisely to throw out someone who plainly is a fan. That is the fallacy.
  2. B is an opinion about quality; it says nothing about who counts as a fan.
  3. C is a neutral remark about production.
  4. D is a slippery slope — a different fallacy.
Answer — A — “Real anime fans only watch subtitled versions…”.
Common slip. Picking D because it too is a fallacy. The question asks for one fallacy in particular.
8 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q18 mark done
Recognise it by: Slippery slope: a chain of unproven “and then”s

A slippery slope fallacy occurs when someone assumes that one event will inevitably lead to a series of increasingly extreme consequences, without sufficient evidence for each step in the chain.

During a school debate, Priya argues: “If we allow students to use calculators in math exams, they will stop learning basic arithmetic. Eventually, they won't be able to solve any problem without a device, and the entire education system will collapse.”

What is Priya doing wrong in her reasoning?

  1. She is rejecting a useful academic tool without considering its benefits.
  2. She is assuming that one policy change will inevitably lead to a series of drastic negative outcomes.
  3. She is generalising the behaviour of all students based on a few poor performers.
  4. She is treating calculator use and arithmetic learning as mutually exclusive skills.

How to see it

The definition is printed; find the option that restates it for Priya's chain (calculators → no arithmetic → dependence → collapse).

Working

  1. Each link is asserted, none evidenced, and the end point is extreme — the shape of a slippery slope.
  2. B describes exactly that.
  3. A and D may be fair criticisms, but they are not the reasoning error the question defines; C describes a generalisation she does not make.
Answer — B — one change assumed to lead inevitably to drastic outcomes.
Common slip. Choosing D, which is a real weakness (false dichotomy) but not the one named.
9 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q19 mark done
Recognise it by: The same item as Q13 — the same answer

Many cities across India have responded to rising road accidents by imposing stricter traffic fines and vehicle penalties for speeding and rash driving. Traffic authorities argue that heavy penalties deter dangerous behaviour and reduce accident rates quickly. However, a study comparing cities in two states found that accident rates declined most in cities that invested in driver awareness campaigns, improved road design with better signage and safety features, and educated young riders through school-based road safety programmes — even when those cities spent less on enforcement and fines. Penalty-based approaches create anger among drivers, encourage bribery, and fail to address why people drive recklessly in the first place. Approaches such as driver education, community awareness campaigns, and safer road infrastructure address the root causes of accidents and build lasting safety habits.

Based on the principles demonstrated in the passage above, if a school applied this same approach to reduce classroom disruptions and student misbehaviour, which of the following would be a critical assumption for the plan's success?

  1. Classroom disruptions stem from lack of guidance and understanding rather than deliberate defiance.
  2. Strict punishment deters student misbehaviour more effectively than awareness and education programmes.
  3. Teachers will require extensive training before implementing awareness-based behaviour management systems.
  4. Teachers should blame parents entirely for not disciplining students at home adequately.

How to see it

This is a reprint of Q13, so the reasoning is identical: the approach fixes root causes by education, so it relies on the cause being educable.

Working

  1. Negate A: if disruptions are deliberate defiance, guidance fails — so A is the critical assumption.
  2. B contradicts the approach; C is helpful but not critical; D is irrelevant blame.
  3. In the paper this item sits after three unrelated questions, so “the passage above” refers back to the road-safety passage before Q12.
Answer — A — disruptions stem from lack of guidance, not deliberate defiance.
Common slip. Hunting for a different answer because a repeated question looks like a trap.
Careful — the paper itself. Q19 is printed word for word as Q13, under a passage that is no longer above it. It is a slip in the sample paper, not a trick; answer it as Q13.
10 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q20 mark done
Recognise it by: Percentages that don't add to 100 force an overlap — or a gap

A survey of 900 teenagers across India examined their music listening preferences. Overall, 78% of teenagers prefer listening to music on YouTube, whilst 60% prefer Spotify. Among teenagers who prefer Spotify, 82% also listen to music on YouTube occasionally. (The data are hypothetical.)

Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the data given?

  1. Most teenagers who prefer Spotify do not use YouTube for music.
  2. There are teenagers who use YouTube but do not use Spotify.
  3. Most teenagers who prefer YouTube do not also prefer Spotify for music.
  4. Teenagers who use both platforms are likely to spend more time listening to music overall.

How to see it

Compare the two totals. If 78% are on YouTube but only 60% on Spotify, at least 18% must be on YouTube and not Spotify.

Working

  1. A contradicts the data: 82% of Spotify users also use YouTube.
  2. C: the YouTube–Spotify overlap is at least 78 + 60 − 100 = 38%, which is about half the YouTube group, so “most” cannot be concluded.
  3. D is about listening time, which the survey never measured.
  4. B: YouTube 78% exceeds Spotify 60%, so at least 18% (about 162 teenagers) are on YouTube without Spotify. It must be true.
Answer — B — some teenagers use YouTube but not Spotify.
Common slip. Reaching for D because it sounds plausible. “Best supported” means forced by the numbers.
11 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2026 paper, SNUSAT Q1 mark done
Recognise it by: Which evidence is needed, not merely related

Niyati wants to understand how safe women in her country feel. She finds some resources online.

P – A book about women Prime Ministers that the country has had.
Q – A documentary about women's experiences using public transportation.
R – A detailed report about the participation of women in the police force.
S – An article discussing the laws that protect women's rights in the workforce.

Which of the following (combinations of) resources will she DEFINITELY need in order to get the most accurate information?

  1. P and Q
  2. Only Q
  3. Only S
  4. P, R and S

How to see it

The question is about a feeling, and only one of the four sources reports what women themselves experienced.

Working

  1. P counts women Prime Ministers, R counts women in the police, S describes workplace law. All three measure women's position, not their sense of safety.
  2. Q is a documentary of women's own experiences of using public transport — first-hand testimony about feeling safe or unsafe.
  3. “DEFINITELY need” asks which source cannot be dispensed with, not which ones are on topic.
Answer — B — only Q.
Common slip. Treating representation (women PMs, women police) as a proxy for safety. It may correlate; it is not evidence of how anyone feels.
12 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2026 paper, SNUSAT Q2 mark done
Recognise it by: What the passage commits itself to

Adriana Petryna, in a book about the Chernobyl nuclear disaster, coined the term “Biological Citizenship”. This refers to the ways in which Ukranian citizens in Chernobyl-affected regions negotiate with state institutions based on their perceived levels of radiation exposure, to avail the benefits that are, on paper, offered to all citizens. For instance, some may undergo complex medical examinations and tests to prove their radiation exposure and establish their eligibility for state-provided compensation as “Chernobyl-sufferers”. One's citizenship status, generally, comes with certain rights and guaranteed access to state amenities.

Based on the above passage, what does citizenship DEFINITELY mean for “Chernobyl-sufferers” in Ukraine?

  1. They can become political citizens only once they have proven their suffering.
  2. They have access to only biological citizenship, not political citizenship.
  3. The benefits of citizenship are dependent on their ability to prove suffering.
  4. The benefits of citizenship are only easily available to non-sufferers of Chernobyl.

How to see it

Find the sentence the passage actually asserts, and strip off everything it merely suggests.

Working

  1. The passage says benefits are “on paper” offered to all, but must be negotiated by proving exposure. That is exactly option C.
  2. A and B talk about becoming a citizen or losing political citizenship — the passage never says the status itself is at stake, only access to benefits.
  3. D reverses the passage: nothing is said about how easily non-sufferers get benefits.
Answer — C — the benefits of citizenship depend on being able to prove suffering.
Common slip. Sliding from “benefits are hard to get” to “citizenship is withheld”. A DEFINITELY question punishes exactly that step.
13 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2026 paper, SNUSAT Q3 mark done
Recognise it by: Strengthen — support both halves of the claim

K-pop (Korean popular music) as the global phenomenon we know it to be wouldn't exist without a combination of democracy and television.

Which of the following historical statements, if true, strengthens the above argument the most?

  1. The Constitution of Republic of Korea, adopted in 1948, guaranteed rights and freedoms for its citizens, and strongly curbs official censorship.
  2. The history of K-pop has a definitive start date, thanks to a band called Seo Taiji and Boys who challenged the dominance of national TV networks.
  3. After South Korea became democratic, broadcast networks in the country were expanded, giving citizens more choices in the media they consumed.
  4. As of 1992, TV was common in 99 percent of South Korean homes, and viewership was highest on the weekends, when the talent shows took place.

How to see it

The claim joins two things. The strongest support is the option that joins the same two things.

Working

  1. The argument is a conjunction: democracy and television.
  2. A is about democracy alone; D is about television alone. Each supports half the claim, so each is weaker than an option covering both.
  3. B actually cuts the other way — it has K-pop starting by defying the TV networks.
  4. C states that democratisation caused broadcasting to expand: the two factors in one causal chain.
Answer — C — democratisation expanded broadcasting.
Common slip. Picking the option with the most impressive statistic (D's 99%). Relevance beats magnitude in a strengthen question.
14 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2026 paper, SNUSAT Q4 mark done
Recognise it by: Main claim = what the example is an example of

Wikipedia is considered as a largely unreliable site in academic circles. However, in 2023, a small change on every Wikipedia page for birds showed their taxonomy to be “Clade:Dinosauria”, essentially indicating that the birds we see around us are heavily modified and evolved dinosaurs. This tiny change was taken as a huge win by modern paleontologists, who claimed that this addition to the most popular website on the internet publicly reflected a whole new, informed evolutionary line of thinking that is otherwise overlooked.

Which of the following best describes the main claim of the above passage?

  1. Public information websites can play a crucial role in delivering scientific research to us.
  2. Unlike other academics, paleontologists consider Wikipedia to be a credible source.
  3. Sharing public information and knowledge is an integral part of scientific research.
  4. Wikipedia is not necessarily reliable since it overlooks new scientific discovery.

How to see it

Ask what the bird example is illustrating; the main claim is the general statement, not the anecdote.

Working

  1. The paleontologists' win is that the finding reached the most popular website on the internet — reach is the point.
  2. B overstates: they welcomed one edit, which is not the same as calling Wikipedia credible.
  3. C is a claim about how research is done; the passage is about how research gets delivered.
  4. D contradicts the passage, which has Wikipedia carrying the new discovery.
Answer — A — public information websites can carry scientific research to the public.
Common slip. C is the nearest miss and reads well on its own. It fails because the passage never claims sharing is part of doing the research.
15 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2026 paper, SNUSAT Q5 mark done
Recognise it by: Name the fallacy, then match it exactly

The ad hominem fallacy is a logical fallacy that involves attacking a person's character instead of their argument.

Which of the following scenarios represents an Ad Hominem Fallacy?

  1. Dan and Steve are debating over a book, and Steve says that he didn't enjoy the story at all.
  2. Rachel argues against using plastic straws, and Sam replies with statistics on waste management.
  3. Maria suggests recycling to help the environment, but Jamie dismisses her because she failed science class.
  4. Paul suggests a new policy at work, and Linda responds by discussing the effectiveness of the current policy.

How to see it

Look for a reply that rejects the person and never touches the proposal.

Working

  1. C: Jamie's reply is about Maria's school record, not about recycling. That is the definition, applied.
  2. B and D are both proper replies — evidence and a counter-proposal.
  3. A is just a difference of taste, not an argument at all.
Answer — C — Jamie dismisses Maria over a failed science class.
Common slip. Reading “attacks the person” as “is rude”. The test is whether the reason offered is about the person.
16 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2026 paper, SNUSAT Q6 mark done
Recognise it by: Two percentages on different bases

Energy policy analysts are evaluating two seemingly contradictory reports on electricity consumption:

Report 1: 60% of the total electricity consumed last year in the country was from urban areas, meaning 40% came from rural regions.
Report 2: Renewable energy sources accounted for 55% of all electricity consumed in rural areas last year.

If both reports are accurate, which of the following must logically be true?

  1. Urban areas had lower rates of renewable energy use compared to rural areas last year.
  2. Rural areas reduced their non-renewable energy consumption by more than 20% compared to the previous year.
  3. The percentage of the country's total renewable energy that was consumed in urban areas was less than 60% last year.
  4. The total amount of electricity from renewable sources consumed in rural areas exceeded that consumed in urban areas last year.

How to see it

Put both reports on the same base — national electricity — before comparing anything.

Working

  1. Rural renewable = 55% of 40% = 22% of the national total. That is the only number the two reports together give you.
  2. Urban renewable is 60% × u, where u is the unknown urban renewable share. Nothing pins u.
  3. B needs last year's figures, which are not given; A and D both need u.
  4. Urban's share of national renewables is 0·6u ÷ (0·6u + 0·22), which stays under 60% as long as u < 55% — that is, as long as urban take-up has not overtaken rural's own 55%.
Answer — C — urban held under 60% of the country's renewable electricity.
Common slip. Comparing 55% with 60% directly. They are percentages of different things: one of rural electricity, the other of national electricity.
Careful — the paper itself. C is the key's answer and the only option in the right territory, but it is not strictly forced: it follows only while urban renewable penetration stays below the rural figure of 55%. Treat it as the best answer rather than a proof.
17 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2026 paper, SNUSAT Q7 mark done
Recognise it by: Match the policy to the stated goal

The Gini Index measures income inequality within a country, with 0 representing perfect equality and 100 representing maximum inequality. Countries with a Gini Index above 40 face increasing inequality and related socio-economic challenges.

Which of the following policy measures would BEST address income inequality while promoting sustainable development in South Africa, which has a Gini Index of 63?

  1. Increasing taxes on luxury goods and services in urban areas.
  2. Subsidizing agricultural production to support rural income generation.
  3. Focusing on deregulating businesses to stimulate economic growth and job creation.
  4. Implementing progressive taxation and directing revenue toward universal healthcare, education, and social security programs.

How to see it

The question sets two targets — inequality and sustainable development. Only one option hits both.

Working

  1. D redistributes at the top (progressive tax) and builds capability at the bottom (health, education, social security). Both halves of the question.
  2. A and B each touch one sector only; neither is a general attack on a Gini of 63.
  3. C addresses growth, which can raise inequality rather than lower it.
Answer — D — progressive taxation funding health, education and social security.
Common slip. Choosing A because taxing luxury “sounds redistributive”. It is narrow, and it does nothing for the bottom of the distribution.
18 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2026 paper, SNUSAT Q8 mark done
Recognise it by: Maximise one group — what must sit elsewhere?
Group text. Cars A, B, C and D are the only vehicles allowed to participate in a racing event. Drivers Karan, Lavanya and Mohsin are the only certified drivers, each assigned to a vehicle. Co-drivers Nikhil, Omar and Priya are the only certified co-drivers taking part.
  1. Every participating car must have a qualified driver onboard.
  2. Only certified drivers and co-drivers are permitted to participate.
  3. Karan will only drive either Car A or Car D.
  4. Nikhil will only co-drive either Car B or Car C.

If Car D accommodates as many drivers and co-drivers as possible, how many participants will be in it?

  1. Exactly two participants
  2. Exactly three participants
  3. Exactly four participants
  4. Exactly five participants

How to see it

All six people take part, so ask who is barred from D — and who has to go with them.

Working

  1. Nikhil can only co-drive B or C, so he is not in D.
  2. Whichever of B or C Nikhil is in must have a driver (rule 1), so one of the three drivers is spent there.
  3. That leaves for D: two drivers, plus Omar and Priya.
  4. Karan may be one of them, since rule 3 allows him Car D.
Answer — C — exactly four.
Common slip. Answering five by forgetting that Nikhil's car still needs a driver. Nikhil costs D two people, not one.
19 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2026 paper, SNUSAT Q9 mark done
Recognise it by: Test each option against all the rules
Group text. Cars A, B, C and D are the only vehicles allowed to participate in a racing event. Drivers Karan, Lavanya and Mohsin are the only certified drivers, each assigned to a vehicle. Co-drivers Nikhil, Omar and Priya are the only certified co-drivers taking part.
  1. Every participating car must have a qualified driver onboard.
  2. Only certified drivers and co-drivers are permitted to participate.
  3. Karan will only drive either Car A or Car D.
  4. Nikhil will only co-drive either Car B or Car C.

If Car A is used, its team could include which of the following members?

  1. Lavanya, Nikhil, Omar, Priya
  2. Karan, Lavanya, Omar, Priya
  3. Lavanya, Mohsin, Omar, Priya
  4. Karan, Lavanya, Mohsin, Priya

How to see it

A “could be” question is killed by a single rule; check rule 4 and the driver supply.

Working

  1. A puts Nikhil in Car A — rule 4 forbids it.
  2. C and D leave Nikhil needing a car (B or C) with no driver free for it: in C both remaining drivers are in A and Karan must take A or D; in D all three drivers are in A.
  3. B works: Karan and Lavanya in A, Mohsin driving B or C with Nikhil.
Answer — B — Karan, Lavanya, Omar, Priya.
Common slip. Checking only the rule about the people named, and not whether the people left over can still be placed legally.
20 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2026 paper, SNUSAT Q10 mark done
Recognise it by: “Must be true” — find the forced move
Group text. Cars A, B, C and D are the only vehicles allowed to participate in a racing event. Drivers Karan, Lavanya and Mohsin are the only certified drivers, each assigned to a vehicle. Co-drivers Nikhil, Omar and Priya are the only certified co-drivers taking part.
  1. Every participating car must have a qualified driver onboard.
  2. Only certified drivers and co-drivers are permitted to participate.
  3. Karan will only drive either Car A or Car D.
  4. Nikhil will only co-drive either Car B or Car C.

If Mohsin and Priya are the only participants in one of the cars, which of the following must be true?

  1. Nikhil, Omar, and Lavanya drive together.
  2. Nikhil drives with Lavanya.
  3. Omar drives with Karan.
  4. Nikhil drives with Omar.

How to see it

Remove the pair that is fixed, then see who is left to satisfy rule 4.

Working

  1. Mohsin and Priya are used up. The drivers left are Karan and Lavanya.
  2. Nikhil must be in B or C, and that car needs a driver.
  3. Karan can only drive A or D, so the driver with Nikhil must be Lavanya.
  4. Omar is then free to go with either, so A, C and D are possible but not forced.
Answer — B — Nikhil drives with Lavanya.
Common slip. Settling for an arrangement that works. “Must be true” needs the statement that holds in every arrangement.
21 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2025 paper, SNUSAT Q1 mark done
Recognise it by: Strengthen the conclusion, not the premise

The most adverse consequences of climate change are not far off. Recent DNA analysis shows that two distinct populations of octopus species, one in the Weddell Sea and the other in the Ross Sea, mated about 125,000 years ago during the last interglacial. This could only have happened if the massive ice sheet (which is West Antarctica) that separates those populations wasn't there at the time. If the South Pole unfroze then, it is very likely to happen this time around too.

interglacial — a geological interval of warmer global average temperature lasting thousands of years, separating two glacial periods (we are currently in an interglacial).

Which of the following assertions, if true, strengthens the above argument?

  1. Due to increasing temperatures, Antarctica is witnessing the spread of a red-green algae for the very first time since its discovery.
  2. In the last interglacial, sea levels were 5 to 10 meters higher than today, indicating that Antarctica lost significant amounts of ice.
  3. West Antarctica, due to being thinner than the East, is likely to melt much faster if global temperatures rise.
  4. Many animals in the Antarctic marine ecosystem have evolved considerably since the last interglacial.

How to see it

Split the argument into the historical premise and the present-day prediction, and ask which half still needs help.

Working

  1. Premise: the ice sheet was gone 125,000 years ago. The DNA evidence already establishes that.
  2. Conclusion: it is very likely to happen this time around too — a claim about now.
  3. B reinforces the premise, which was not in doubt, so it adds least.
  4. A reports change happening in Antarctica now, which is what the prediction needs.
  5. D weakens the analogy if anything; C is a mechanism, not evidence that it is under way.
Answer — A — present-day evidence that Antarctica is already changing.
Common slip. Reaching for the option that best supports the fact you have just read. A strengthener should attack the weakest link, and the weak link here is the leap from then to now.
22 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2025 paper, SNUSAT Q2 mark done
Recognise it by: Whose argument is being asked for?

Micro trends are fashion pieces, often inspired by celebrities and influencers, that are only meant to last the duration of a fashion season. They experience a surge in popularity before fading just as quickly — meaning there is sudden mass production of particular items in demand, and this demand fades just as quickly. Many people oppose mass participation in some micro trends, claiming that this can cause adverse effects that damage the social, economic or environmental ecosystems irreparably.

Which of the following is MOST LIKELY to be an argument against such micro trends made by these critics?

  1. They contribute a huge amount of waste in landfills in a short duration of time.
  2. They are always expensive and cannot be bought by a large number of people.
  3. They are not comfortable or suited to the culture and climate of all places in the world.
  4. They provide constant avenues of employment for factory workers and delivery agents.

How to see it

The passage names the grounds the critics use. Pick the option that lands on one of them.

Working

  1. The critics' stated worry is damage to “social, economic or environmental ecosystems”, and the passage's own mechanism is mass production followed by collapsing demand.
  2. A is exactly that mechanism's consequence: goods made fast, discarded fast.
  3. B (“always expensive”) contradicts the mass-production premise.
  4. C is a complaint about taste, not damage. D is an argument for.
Answer — A — landfill waste in a short time.
Common slip. Option D is a real effect of micro trends, and it is on topic. It is simply on the other side of the argument.
23 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2025 paper, SNUSAT Q3 mark done
Recognise it by: Reverse-engineer the definition from the reasons given

There is some debate amongst historians whether the development of agriculture in human societies fits into the standard definition of a “revolution”. Proponents of the agricultural revolution argue that it resulted in the invention of the first cities, allowed for industrialization, and caused the human population to grow massively, and these massive changes cannot be ignored.

Based on the above argument, what can you DEFINITELY assume to be part of the standard definition of a revolution?

  1. revolutions are inherently violent
  2. revolutions cause a restructuring of human society
  3. revolutions last for short periods of time, such as weeks or months
  4. revolutions are inherently political in nature and are driven by ideology

How to see it

The proponents' reasons only work if the definition contains a particular element. Find that element.

Working

  1. Their reasons are cities, industrialization and population growth — all large-scale changes to how society is organised.
  2. For those reasons to count as reasons, restructuring society must be part of what “revolution” means.
  3. A, C and D are all plausible things revolutions often are, but none of them is needed for the argument to work — and agriculture is neither violent, brief, nor ideological.
Answer — B — revolutions restructure human society.
Common slip. Answering with what revolutions are usually like. The question asks what the argument presupposes.
24 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2025 paper, SNUSAT Q4 mark done
Recognise it by: Chain of escalating consequences = slippery slope

Read the following statement.

“If you go outside without a coat, you will catch a cold and infect the rest of the family. Then your sister will have to miss her classes and she will get a bad grade and eventually, fail her course.”

Which of the following fallacies BEST describes the statement above?

  1. False dilemma: presenting only two options or sides when there could be many
  2. Generalization: arriving at a universal conclusion based on few or insufficient facts
  3. Slippery slope: claiming that an initial event or action will trigger a series of extreme or undesirable outcomes
  4. Ad-hominem: attacking an individual's choices or personal actions/traits rather than focusing on their reasoning

How to see it

Count the links. A fallacy with a chain of then … then … is almost always the slippery slope.

Working

  1. Lay the statement out as a chain: no coat → catches cold → infects the family → sister misses class → bad grade → fails the course.
  2. That is five links, each asserted as if it were certain, ending somewhere far more serious than where it began. Both features are the signature of the slippery slope.
  3. Check the others do not fit: there is no forced choice between two options (A), no leap from a small sample to a universal rule (B), and nobody's character is attacked (D).
  4. Note that each individual link is merely unlikely; the fallacy is in treating the whole chain as inevitable.
Answer — C — slippery slope.
Common slip. Reading “you will catch a cold” as a hasty generalization. The defect is the chain, not the sample size.
25 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2025 paper, SNUSAT Q5 mark done
Recognise it by: Syllogism: what the premises rule out

Two statements about two types of water bodies — lakes and oceans — are followed by three conclusions.

Statement I: All oceans are salty.
Statement II: Lakes and oceans are different water bodies.

Conclusion (i): No lakes are salty.
Conclusion (ii): Lakes may or may not be salty.
Conclusion (iii): No water body can be classified as both a lake and an ocean.

Which of the following conclusions logically follow from Statements I and II?

  1. (i) only
  2. (ii) only
  3. (i) and (iii) only
  4. (ii) and (iii) only

How to see it

“All oceans are salty” says nothing at all about non-oceans.

Working

  1. (i) is the classic inversion error: all oceans are salty does not make saltiness exclusive to oceans. False.
  2. (ii) is exactly the right amount of ignorance — the premises leave lakes open either way. Follows.
  3. (iii) is a restatement of Statement II: being different kinds of water body means nothing is both. Follows.
Answer — D — (ii) and (iii) only.
Common slip. Rejecting (ii) because it “says nothing”. In syllogism questions a conclusion that records uncertainty is often the only valid one.
26 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2025 paper, SNUSAT Q6 mark done
Recognise it by: Cause hunting: which link is economic, not incidental

Rangan, a blacksmith from the Kota tribe in Puddu Kotagiri, Nilgiris, Tamil Nadu, continues a generations-long family trade. However, with tea plantations expanding and replacing millet fields, the demand for blacksmiths has declined. From 1971 to 2008, tea cultivation in the Nilgiris tripled, leading to reduced need for their products.

What is the MOST LIKELY reason for this relationship between tea cultivation and the work of blacksmiths?

  1. A mass migration of people to the Nilgiris resulted in people choosing tea cultivation as their source of income since it was not as laborious as ironwork.
  2. Tea cultivation does not require iron tools such as ploughs or rakes which were essential for the cultivation of millet, hence reducing the demand for iron tools.
  3. The lands over which tea cultivation is spreading were previously lands that belonged to blacksmiths, and the loss of this land meant that they had no place to work.
  4. The soil conditions and fertiliser products required for tea cultivation caused iron tools to rust faster and get damaged more easily, hence making iron tools harder to maintain.

How to see it

The passage says demand fell. Look for the option that removes a customer, not one that removes a worker or a workshop.

Working

  1. Millet is a ploughed crop; tea is a perennial bush that is picked. Replacing one with the other removes the need for ploughs and rakes.
  2. That is a fall in demand, which is what the passage reports.
  3. A explains why people might leave smithing, not why nobody buys from it. C invents land ownership the passage never mentions. D would raise demand for replacements.
Answer — B — tea does not need the iron tools millet did.
Common slip. Option D reads like a sensible mechanism until you notice it predicts the opposite: tools that wear out faster are bought more often.
27 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2025 paper, SNUSAT Q7 mark done
Recognise it by: Find the property the odd ones out share

An ambigram is a word that reads the same when viewed in a mirror (either sideways or upside-down). Dev made a list of ambigrams: WOW, 808, 609, dollop, passed, swims. Of these, he says that WOW and 808 have a special property that sets them apart from the other words in the list.

What is this property likely to be?

  1. their meaning changes if you read them from back to front
  2. they look the same when viewed upside-down in a mirror
  3. they make the same word forwards and backwards
  4. they are the shortest ambigrams in the given list

How to see it

The definition given applies to all six items, so the special property must be something extra. Write each item backwards and compare it with itself.

Working

  1. WOW → WOW and 808 → 808: both are palindromes.
  2. 609 → 906, dollop → pollod, passed → dessap, swims → smiws — none of these reads the same backwards.
  3. So the shared property is being a palindrome, which is what C says.
  4. D is false anyway: 609 has three characters, the same as WOW and 808.
Answer — C — they read the same forwards and backwards.
Common slip. Option B restates the definition of an ambigram, which all six items have. A property that everything on the list shares cannot set two of them apart.
28 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2025 paper, SNUSAT Q8 mark done
Recognise it by: Straw man = misrepresent, then attack the misrepresentation

A straw man argument is a type of fallacy in which one person misrepresents or exaggerates their opponent's position to make it easier to attack or refute. Given below are four invalid arguments. Identify the straw-man argument.

  1. The two people I met from this city have been extremely rude to me, I'm expecting everyone in this city to be arrogant and hostile.
  2. She ate an apple before her exam, and did not score well. Despite this, she kept eating apples and wondering why she was having bad luck.
  3. You should not take his advice on financial planning seriously. His personal finances are in terrible condition and he has been in debt multiple times.
  4. People who argue for reducing the defence budget clearly have no respect for our national security and want to leave our country vulnerable to attacks from enemies.

How to see it

Ask which option restates the opponent's position before attacking it — and restates it wrongly.

Working

  1. D turns “spend less on defence” into “wants the country left defenceless”, then attacks that. Textbook straw man.
  2. A is a hasty generalization (two people → a whole city).
  3. B is a false cause / superstition.
  4. C is ad hominem — and note that it is the nearest miss, because it also attacks rather than argues. The difference is that C attacks the man, D attacks a position he never held.
Answer — D — reducing the defence budget recast as wanting the country undefended.
Common slip. Confusing straw man with ad hominem. Both dodge the argument; only the straw man invents a new one to knock down.
29 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2025 paper, SNUSAT Q9 mark done
Recognise it by: Purpose of a quoted phrase, in context

“Sultana's Dream”, a 1905 feminist utopian novella by Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain, depicts a world where women are in power and men are confined to domestic roles. When the protagonist Sultana enquires about the absence of men in public spaces, Sister Sara says that they are “where they ought to be”. The story challenges conventional gender roles and advocates for women's empowerment. Through this gender-flipped society, the novella encourages readers to envision a world without gender discrimination, offering equal opportunities to all.

What is the MOST LIKELY purpose for Rokeya using the phrase “where they ought to be”?

  1. To imagine a reality where women empower men.
  2. To express her opinion that men need to be confined to the domestic sphere.
  3. To express contempt for the ways in which men carry out public office and social responsibilities.
  4. To highlight the absurdity of the existing societal norms that dictate men's superiority and women's inferiority.

How to see it

The summary tells you the book's aim is a world without discrimination. A reversal written to that aim is satire, not a proposal.

Working

  1. The phrase is one that was, and is, said about women. Put in Sister Sara's mouth about men, it exposes how it sounds.
  2. B takes the satire literally — and contradicts the stated aim of equal opportunities for all.
  3. A and C narrow the target to empowerment or to men's competence; the passage's own words are about discrimination in general.
Answer — D — it exposes the absurdity of the existing norm.
Common slip. Answering B because that is what the sentence says. In a satire the literal reading is the one being mocked.
30 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning 2025 paper, SNUSAT Q10 mark done
Recognise it by: Conditional chain — trace, don't reverse

Here is a statement: When it's not raining, I go for a run. On days when I don't go for a run, I work out at home. After working out at home, I eat two eggs, otherwise I eat one.

Provided this statement is true and is strictly followed, which of the following conditions is likely to occur?

  1. staying home on a sunny day
  2. eating two eggs after a run
  3. working out on a rainy day
  4. eating two eggs on a sunny day

How to see it

Write the three rules as arrows, then test each option against them.

Working

  1. Rule 1: not raining → run. Rule 2: no run → home workout. Rule 3: home workout ↔ two eggs.
  2. A is impossible: a sunny day forces a run, so he is not staying home.
  3. Rule 1 fixes what happens on a clear day but Rule 2 only fires when there is no run — it never forbids working out as well as running.
  4. So on a sunny day he runs, may also work out at home, and then eats two eggs: option D can occur.
Answer — D — eating two eggs on a sunny day. (SNU's key.)
Common slip. Reading the rules as if-and-only-ifs. “When it's not raining I run” says nothing about rainy days, and “when I don't run I work out” does not forbid working out on a running day.
Careful — the paper itself. This one is loose. Under the same reading that makes D possible, B (two eggs after a run) and C (working out on a rainy day) are possible too; under the stricter if-and-only-if reading, C is forced and D is impossible. Only A is ruled out on every reading. Learn the arrow method from it and do not lose time arguing with it in the exam.
31 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning Predicted 2027, SNUSAT V1 mark done
Recognise it by: Only two choices offered when more exist = false dilemma

At a parents' meeting, a trustee says: “Either we ban mobile phones from the school building completely, or our students will never be able to concentrate in class. Since we want them to concentrate, a total ban is the only option.”

Which statement BEST describes the flaw in the trustee's reasoning?

  1. The trustee attacks the parents who disagree instead of their arguments.
  2. The trustee presents two extremes as the only possibilities, ignoring middle options such as phone lockers or class-time rules.
  3. The trustee assumes a ban will lead to a chain of ever worse consequences.
  4. The trustee relies on the opinion of an expert from an unrelated field.

How to see it

Count the options the speaker allows. When an argument says “either X or disaster” and there are obvious options in between, it is a false dilemma.

Working

  1. The trustee offers exactly two possibilities: total ban, or students who can never concentrate.
  2. Many intermediate policies exist — phones handed in at the start of a lesson, lockers, use only at break — and the argument never rules them out.
  3. That is the defining move of a false dilemma (false dichotomy).
  4. A is ad hominem, C is slippery slope, D is a misplaced appeal to authority; the trustee does none of these.
Answer — B — two extremes presented as the only choices.
Common slip. Picking C because the trustee sounds alarmist. A slippery slope needs a chain of steps; here there is a single either/or.
32 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning Predicted 2027, SNUSAT V2 mark done
Recognise it by: Two things rise together ≠ one causes the other

A survey of 5,000 students in 40 schools, using marks taken from board records rather than from the students themselves, found that students who eat dinner with their family at least five nights a week score on average 12% higher in board examinations. The principal of one school announces: “Family dinners raise examination marks. Every parent should start eating dinner with their child.”

Which statement best describes the logical error in the principal's reasoning?

  1. The sample is too small to draw any conclusion about students.
  2. The marks are self-reported and therefore unreliable.
  3. The principal assumes that what holds in 40 schools must hold in her own school.
  4. The principal ignores that a third factor, such as a stable household with more time and support, might produce both regular family dinners and higher marks.

How to see it

The data show an association. A claim that one thing causes another needs the other explanations closed off — and the stem has deliberately closed off every flaw except that one.

Working

  1. The survey is large (5,000 students, 40 schools), so A fails.
  2. The marks come from board records, not from the students, so B fails.
  3. C is not the error: the principal's conclusion is about every parent, and the data are broad enough to describe students in general.
  4. What remains is the jump from goes with to causes: homes where the family eats together nightly may differ in income, routine and parental time, and those could raise marks with or without the dinners. That is D.
Answer — D — correlation taken as causation, with a third factor ignored.
Common slip. Reaching for a generic flaw (small sample, self-report) without checking whether the stem has already ruled it out.
33 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning Predicted 2027, SNUSAT V3 mark done
Recognise it by: Attacks the person, not the argument = ad hominem

In a debate on whether the city should build more cycle lanes, Kabir presents accident data showing that cycle lanes reduce injuries. His opponent replies: “Kabir doesn't even own a car, so of course he wants cycle lanes. We can ignore his figures.”

Which fallacy does the opponent commit?

  1. Ad hominem — rejecting the evidence because of something about the person presenting it.
  2. Straw man — replacing Kabir's argument with a weaker version and attacking that.
  3. Hasty generalisation — drawing a broad rule from a few cases.
  4. Circular reasoning — assuming the conclusion in the premise.

How to see it

Ask what the reply actually engages with. If it says nothing about the data and everything about the speaker, it is ad hominem.

Working

  1. Kabir's argument rests on accident data.
  2. The reply does not question the data, its source or its interpretation; it points to Kabir's own circumstances (no car) and dismisses the figures for that reason.
  3. Whether Kabir owns a car has no bearing on whether the injury figures are true: this is an ad hominem.
  4. A straw man would restate Kabir's argument wrongly; nothing here is restated at all.
Answer — A — ad hominem.
Common slip. Choosing straw man. A straw man misrepresents the argument; an ad hominem ignores it and goes for the arguer.
34 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning Predicted 2027, SNUSAT V4 mark done
Recognise it by: Expertise in one field cited for a claim in another

An advertisement shows a celebrated cricket captain saying: “I have used OrthoRest mattresses for years. Take it from me — they cure back pain permanently.”

Why is the advertisement's reasoning weak?

  1. It assumes that what is true for one mattress is true for all mattresses.
  2. It presents only two choices — OrthoRest or back pain.
  3. It relies on the authority of a person whose expertise is not in medicine or back health.
  4. It attacks rival mattress makers rather than arguing for its own product.

How to see it

A claim about a medical cure needs medical evidence. A famous name stands in for that evidence — the classic misplaced appeal to authority.

Working

  1. The claim — a permanent cure for back pain — is a medical one.
  2. The only support offered is the captain's word and his own experience.
  3. His expertise is cricket, not medicine, so his endorsement does not make a medical claim more likely to be true: appeal to (irrelevant) authority.
  4. A, B and D describe arguments the advertisement does not make: it compares with no other mattresses, names no alternative and attacks no rival.
Answer — C — misplaced appeal to authority.
Common slip. Thinking any testimonial is fine because the person is honest. Honesty is not expertise.
35 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning Predicted 2027, SNUSAT V5 mark done
Recognise it by: Match every part of the definition, not just the topic

Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, notice and remember information that supports what one already believes, while overlooking or dismissing information that contradicts it.

Which of the following situations best represents confirmation bias?

  1. Meera believes her new phone brand is the best; she reads every positive review carefully but skips the negative ones as “paid by rivals”.
  2. Arjun changed his opinion about a film after reading three critical reviews.
  3. Sana forgot her friend's birthday because she was busy with exams.
  4. Dev bought a phone because it was the cheapest one in the shop.

How to see it

The definition has two halves: seeks out what agrees, and dismisses what disagrees. Look for an example that shows both.

Working

  1. A: Meera already holds a belief, attends to the supporting reviews, and dismisses the contrary ones with an excuse. Both halves present.
  2. B: Arjun updated his view on contrary evidence — the opposite of confirmation bias.
  3. C is ordinary forgetting; no belief is being protected.
  4. D is a decision on price, with no prior belief being defended.
Answer — A — Meera reads only what agrees with her.
Common slip. Choosing an option that merely mentions opinions or reviews. The test is the selective treatment of evidence.
36 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning Predicted 2027, SNUSAT V6 mark done
Recognise it by: Assumption = the unstated link the plan cannot work without

A college library will stay open until midnight during the examination month. The librarian argues: “Many students have told us they cannot study at home in the evening. Longer hours will therefore improve examination results.”

Which of the following is a critical assumption of the librarian's argument?

  1. Students who study at home always score lower than those who study in libraries.
  2. Longer opening hours will cost the college very little.
  3. Every student in the college will use the library after 8 pm.
  4. Students who lack an evening study space will actually use the extra hours to study.

How to see it

Negate each candidate. If the argument collapses when it is false, it is the assumption; if the argument survives, it was not needed.

Working

  1. Negate D: those students would not use the extra hours to study. Then the longer hours cannot raise their results, and the argument falls. So D is assumed.
  2. Negate A: some home-studiers do as well as library users. The argument survives — it is only about students who cannot study at home.
  3. Negate B: the hours are expensive. Cost has nothing to do with whether results improve.
  4. Negate C: not every student comes. Results can still improve for those who do. C is far stronger than the argument needs.
Answer — D — the students who need the space will use it to study.
Common slip. Picking the extreme option (C or A). An assumption is the minimum the argument needs, so words like “every” and “always” usually mark a distractor.
37 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning Predicted 2027, SNUSAT V7 mark done
Recognise it by: Weaken a cause: show something else changed at the same time

The city traffic department reports: “Since the Ring Road flyover opened in March, the average morning commute has fallen by 15%. The flyover has clearly solved the city's congestion problem.”

Which of the following, if true, most WEAKENS the department's conclusion?

  1. The flyover was completed three months ahead of schedule.
  2. A new metro line opened in the same month and many commuters switched to it from the roads.
  3. Commuters say they like the view from the flyover.
  4. Other cities that built flyovers also report shorter commutes.

How to see it

A before-and-after claim is weakened most by a rival cause that arrived at the same moment.

Working

  1. The conclusion credits the flyover with the 15% fall.
  2. B gives a different, simultaneous change — the metro — that would shorten commutes on its own by taking cars off the road.
  3. If B is true, the fall cannot be attributed to the flyover with any confidence.
  4. A and C are irrelevant to cause; D, if anything, strengthens the claim.
Answer — B — the metro opened at the same time.
Common slip. Picking D because it is about other cities. It supports the flyover, so it strengthens rather than weakens.
38 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning Predicted 2027, SNUSAT V8 mark done
Recognise it by: Two percentages over 100%: the overlap is forced

In a survey of 1,000 students, 70% said they enjoy watching cricket and 55% said they enjoy watching football.

Note: the data are hypothetical.

Which of the following MUST be true?

  1. Most students who enjoy football also enjoy cricket.
  2. Some students enjoy neither sport.
  3. At least 250 students enjoy both sports.
  4. Exactly 25% of the students enjoy both sports.

How to see it

70% + 55% = 125% of a group that is only 100%, so at least 25% must be counted twice. That much is forced; anything more precise is not.

Working

  1. Cricket 700, football 550, total 1,000.
  2. 700 + 550 − 1,000 = 250, so at least 250 enjoy both. C must be true.
  3. D is not forced: the overlap could be anywhere from 250 to 550.
  4. A: if only 250 enjoy both, then 250 of the 550 football fans (45%) like cricket — not most. B: if the overlap is exactly 250, everyone enjoys at least one sport, so nobody enjoys neither.
Answer — C — at least 250 enjoy both.
Common slip. Choosing D. The 25% is a minimum, not a measured value.
39 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning Predicted 2027, SNUSAT V9 mark done
Recognise it by: If P then Q; not Q ⇒ not P (contrapositive)

The rules of a school sports day are:

  • If it rains, the football final is cancelled.
  • If the football final is cancelled, ticket refunds are issued.

On the day, no ticket refunds were issued.

Which of the following must be true?

  1. It did not rain.
  2. The football final was cancelled for some other reason.
  3. It rained, but the final was played anyway.
  4. If refunds had been issued, it must have rained.

How to see it

Chain the rules: rain ⇒ cancelled ⇒ refunds. Then read the chain backwards with every term negated — the contrapositive.

Working

  1. Combined rule: rain ⇒ refunds.
  2. Contrapositive: no refunds ⇒ no cancellation ⇒ no rain.
  3. B and C contradict the rules: a cancellation would have triggered refunds, and rain would have triggered a cancellation.
  4. D is affirming the consequent: refunds could follow a cancellation for some other reason, so refunds do not prove rain.
Answer — A — it did not rain.
Common slip. D reverses the arrow. “If P then Q” never licenses “if Q then P”.
40 of 40 SNUSAT · Logical Reasoning Predicted 2027, SNUSAT V10 mark done
Recognise it by: The conclusion is what the evidence is offered for

Several state governments have tried to cut plastic waste by fining shops that hand out plastic bags. Fines produce a quick drop, but within a year bag use often creeps back as enforcement slackens. Towns that also set up deposit-return schemes, made cloth bags cheaply available at shop counters, and ran school campaigns on waste have kept bag use low for years, even where fines were small. Habits change when the easy choice is also the right one.

Which of the following best states the author's main conclusion?

  1. Fines on plastic bags should be abolished.
  2. School campaigns are the only effective way to reduce plastic waste.
  3. Enforcement always slackens within a year.
  4. Making alternatives easy and building awareness reduces plastic use more lastingly than fines alone.

How to see it

Find the sentence the rest of the passage is evidence for. Then reject options that say more (“only”, “abolish”) or less than the passage.

Working

  1. The passage contrasts fines (a short-lived drop) with a package of measures (lasting reduction), and closes with the general principle behind the package.
  2. D states exactly that contrast — it is the claim the examples support.
  3. A goes too far: the passage never says fines should go, only that they are not enough on their own.
  4. B singles out one part of the package and adds “only”; C turns a supporting detail (“often”) into an absolute.
Answer — D — easy alternatives plus awareness beat fines alone.
Common slip. Picking a true-sounding detail from the passage. The main conclusion is the claim, not one of the pieces of evidence for it.
2

SNUSAT · Quantitative Aptitude

Ratio, percentage, mensuration and data reading — at class 9-10 level, but wrapped in a diagram, a flowchart or a pattern you have to decode first.

40 questions · 10 from the 2027 paper, 10 from 2026, 10 from 2025, then 10 predicted variations
1 of 40 SNUSAT · Quantitative Aptitude 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q1 mark done
Recognise it by: Batch size = rate × time; then divide what is left by the rate

A machine produces toys at the rate of t toys per hour, where t > 1. It takes 6 hours to produce an entire batch of toys. If the machine has already produced 4 toys, how many more hours are required to complete the entire batch?

  1. t − 4
  2. 6t − 4
  3. 6 − 4t
  4. 6 − 4/t

How to see it

Work in toys first, hours last. The batch is a number of toys; turn the toys still owed back into hours by dividing by the rate.

Working

  1. Whole batch = rate × time = 6t toys.
  2. Still to make: 6t − 4 toys.
  3. Time for those = (6t − 4)/t = 6 − 4/t hours.
  4. Sanity check with t = 4: a 24-toy batch, 4 done, 20 left at 4 an hour is 5 hours, and 6 − 4/4 = 5. ✓
Answer — D — 6 − 4/t.
Common slip. Choosing B, which is the number of toys left, not the hours.
2 of 40 SNUSAT · Quantitative Aptitude 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q2 mark done
Recognise it by: Split the total time between the two kinds of road; ignore the decoy

Aryan is competing in an 800 m cycling race, which consists of two types of sections:

  • Even road: on these smooth stretches Aryan rides at a constant speed of 5 m/s.
  • Uneven sections: each uneven section spans 6 m, and the total time Aryan spends crossing all these sections is exactly 50 seconds.

After every 200 m of the race, the number of uneven sections in the next 200 m is halved compared to the previous 200 m.

If Aryan completes the race in 2 minutes 54 seconds, what is the total number of uneven sections he crossed?

  1. 5
  2. 15
  3. 25
  4. 30

How to see it

The total time and the uneven time are both given, so the even-road time follows, and with it the even distance. The halving rule is only a consistency check.

Working

  1. Total time = 2 min 54 s = 174 s. Time on even road = 174 − 50 = 124 s.
  2. Even distance = 5 × 124 = 620 m, so the uneven sections cover 800 − 620 = 180 m.
  3. Number of sections = 180 / 6 = 30.
  4. Check against the halving rule: 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 30, so the four 200 m blocks can indeed hold them. ✓
Answer — D — 30.
Common slip. Trying to use the halving rule to find the count. It cannot fix the total on its own; the time data do.
3 of 40 SNUSAT · Quantitative Aptitude 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q3 mark done
Recognise it by: Lost → played → total: three fractions, applied in order

In an inter-school tennis championship held in a state, Santa Public School played 2⁄3 of the total number of matches played. In the matches the school played, the ratio of the number of matches it won to the number of matches it lost was 2 : 1.

If the school lost 6 of the matches it played, the total number of matches played in the championship was

  1. 9.
  2. 12.
  3. 18.
  4. 27.

How to see it

Walk outwards: losses give the school's matches, and the school's matches are a known fraction of the championship.

Working

  1. Won : lost = 2 : 1 and lost = 6, so won = 12.
  2. Matches the school played = 12 + 6 = 18.
  3. 18 is 2⁄3 of the total, so the total = 18 × 3/2 = 27.
  4. The printed key's 12 is the number of matches the school won — one step into the problem, not the end of it.
Answer — D (27) by the working; the key says B.
Common slip. Stopping at 12 (matches won) or 18 (matches the school played).
Careful — the paper itself. SNU's key gives B, 12. That cannot be the championship total: the school alone played 18 matches. 12 is the number it won. In the exam the key is what scores, but learn the method that gives 27.
4 of 40 SNUSAT · Quantitative Aptitude 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q4 mark done
Recognise it by: Only the part that changed changes the total

The cost of a metro rail project was estimated at Rs 8000 crores of which 15% was the land cost. By the time of execution of the project, the land price increased by 20%.

What is the increase in the estimated project cost only due to the increase in the land price?

  1. Rs 240 crores
  2. Rs 400 crores
  3. Rs 1600 crores
  4. Rs 2800 crores

How to see it

A percentage of a percentage: 20% of the 15% slice, not 20% of the whole.

Working

  1. Land cost = 15% of 8000 = 1200 crores.
  2. Its increase = 20% of 1200 = 240 crores.
  3. Equivalently 0.15 × 0.20 = 3% of 8000 = 240.
Answer — A — Rs 240 crores.
Common slip. C is 20% of the whole project. The rest of the cost did not move.
5 of 40 SNUSAT · Quantitative Aptitude 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q5 mark done
Recognise it by: A repeating tile must carry the pattern's black-to-white ratio

Shown below is part of a pattern on a cloth.

  1. only P
  2. only Q
  3. both P and Q
  4. neither P nor Q

How to see it

Before fitting shapes, count colours. Any tile that repeats to make the pattern must have the same share of black pentagons as the pattern itself.

Working

  1. The cloth is a pentagon tiling in which every black pentagon is surrounded by whites: one pentagon in four is black.
  2. P has four pentagons, one black — ratio 1 : 3, matching the cloth. It is the four-pentagon group (a stretched hexagon) that repeats across the fabric, and translating it fills the plane with the black ones in the right places.
  3. Q has four pentagons, two black — ratio 1 : 1. However it is repeated, half the cloth would be black, which it is not.
  4. So only P works.
Answer — A — only P.
Common slip. Matching Q because its black pentagons look like the cloth's. Check the ratio first — it rejects Q in seconds.
6 of 40 SNUSAT · Quantitative Aptitude 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q6 mark done
Recognise it by: Write both perimeters in the breadth b

Aakash has 2 similar rectangular sheets of paper as shown in Figure 1 and Figure 2. The length of each rectangular sheet is twice its breadth. He cuts both the sheets into two equal pieces — one of them lengthwise and the other breadthwise as shown.

If the perimeter of each piece in Figure 1 is 60 cm, what is the perimeter of each piece in Figure 2?

  1. 36 cm
  2. 40 cm
  3. 48 cm
  4. 60 cm

How to see it

Let the breadth be b, so the length is 2b. Each cut halves one side.

Working

  1. Figure 1 cut lengthwise: each piece is 2b by b/2, perimeter 2(2b + b/2) = 5b = 60, so b = 12 cm.
  2. Figure 2 cut breadthwise: each piece is b by b, a square.
  3. Its perimeter = 4b = 48 cm.
Answer — C — 48 cm.
Common slip. Assuming equal halves have equal perimeters (D). Area is shared equally; perimeter is not.
7 of 40 SNUSAT · Quantitative Aptitude 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q7 mark done
Recognise it by: Equal counts per type ⇒ call each count n

A math test had only two-mark, five-mark and ten-mark questions. Each of these types had the same number of questions.

¼ of all the five-mark questions and ⅓ of all the ten-mark questions were from algebra. There were no two-mark questions from algebra.

What fraction of the total number of questions in the test were from algebra?

  1. 7/36
  2. 7/12
  3. 1/12
  4. (Cannot say without knowing the total number of questions.)

How to see it

A fraction of a fraction does not need the actual number; let it be n and it cancels.

Working

  1. Each type has n questions, so the test has 3n.
  2. Algebra = n/4 + n/3 = 7n/12.
  3. Fraction = (7n/12) / 3n = 7/36.
Answer — A — 7/36.
Common slip. Answering 7/12 — that is algebra as a fraction of one type's count, forgetting there are three types.
8 of 40 SNUSAT · Quantitative Aptitude 2027 paper, SNUSAT Q8 mark done
Recognise it by: Symmetric runs of integers cancel; keep only what sticks out

The sum of the consecutive integers from (−30) to 200 is u.

What is the sum of the consecutive integers from (−200) to 32?

  1. (−u) + 63
  2. (−u) + 2
  3. u + 63
  4. u + 2

How to see it

−30 to 30 sums to zero, so u is really 31 + … + 200. Do the same trick on the second run.

Working

  1. u = (−30 + … + 30) + (31 + … + 200) = 31 + … + 200.
