Recognise it by: First orbit holds exactly one wavelength

For an electron in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen, which expression represents its de Broglie wavelength?

  1. πr
  2. 2πr
  3. πr/h
  4. 2πr/h

How to see it

Bohr's condition is a standing-wave condition: the circumference holds n whole wavelengths.

Working

  1. mvr = nh/2π and λ = h/mv combine to 2πr = nλ.
  2. For n = 1: λ = 2πr.
  3. C and D have the wrong units (length divided by J s).
Answer — B — 2πr.
Common slip. Writing πr by halving the circumference.
10 of 40 APT · Physics 2027 paper, APT Physics Q10 mark done
Recognise it by: Curvature direction gives the sign; radius mv/qB gives the mass

Three particles P, Q and R enter a region of uniform magnetic field (into the page) at the same speed, perpendicular to the field. Their paths are shown. What are P, Q and R likely to be?

  1. P alpha, Q positron, R electron
  2. P electron, Q positron, R alpha
  3. P positron, Q alpha, R electron
  4. P electron, Q alpha, R positron

How to see it

Use F = qv × B to sort the charges by sign, then r = mv/qB to tell a light particle from a heavy one.

Working

  1. Particles move up the page, B into it: v × B points left. P and Q curve left ⇒ positive; R curves right ⇒ negative: R is the electron.
  2. Radius ∝ m/q: positron m/e, alpha 4mp/2e = 2mp/e — thousands of times larger.
  3. Q has the wider arc (alpha); P has the tight arc, matching the electron's R in size — the positron, which has the electron's mass and opposite charge.
Answer — C — P positron, Q alpha, R electron.
Common slip. Getting the sign backwards by using the left-hand rule for a force on a positive charge as if it were for electrons.
11 of 40 APT · Physics 2026 paper, APT Physics Q1 mark done
Recognise it by: Refraction at the water surface bends rays towards the normal

A point light source is positioned directly above a plastic disc. In the first scenario the disc floats on the surface of water in a bucket, the water's depth being h. In the second the water is removed and the disc is held at the same height h above the bottom of the bucket.

Which option accurately compares the area of the shadow cast by the disc on the bottom of the bucket in Scenario 1 (with water) with that in Scenario 2 (empty)?

  1. The area of the shadow is larger in scenario 1.
  2. The area of the shadow is smaller in scenario 1.
  3. The area of the shadow is the same in both scenarios.
  4. (Cannot determine the area of the shadow cast without knowing the specific value of h and the area of the disc.)

How to see it

Follow one edge ray. The shadow's edge is set by the ray that just grazes the rim of the disc.

Working

  1. In the empty bucket the grazing ray travels in a straight line from the source past the rim to the floor, spreading out as it goes — the shadow is larger than the disc.
  2. With water, that same ray enters the water at the surface, going from a rarer to a denser medium, so it bends towards the normal — that is, towards the vertical.
  3. Bending towards the vertical means it reaches the floor closer to the axis than it would have done.
  4. Every edge ray is pulled inwards the same way, so the shadow's rim closes in: the shadow is smaller with water.
Answer — B — the shadow is smaller in Scenario 1.
Common slip. Thinking about apparent depth (the floor looks raised) instead of about where the rays actually land. The shadow is drawn by real rays, not by the image.
12 of 40 APT · Physics 2026 paper, APT Physics Q2 mark done
Recognise it by: τ = I A B sinθ — and here sinθ = 1, so compare areas

Three loops, each carrying a current I, are placed in a uniform magnetic field B as shown. Compare the torque experienced by the loops.

  1. τ1 < τ2 = τ3
  2. τ1 < τ2 < τ3
  3. τ1 = τ2 > τ3
  4. τ1 = τ2 = τ3

How to see it

Shape is irrelevant to the torque on a plane loop — only the area it encloses matters. So count squares.

Working

  1. τ = m × B with m = IA, so τ = I A B sinθ where θ is between the normal and B.
  2. All three loops lie in the plane of the page and B lies in that plane too, so every normal is perpendicular to B: θ = 90° and sinθ = 1 for all three. Torque is then just I A B.
  3. Counting grid squares: loop 1 is 2 × 2 = 4; loop 2 is an L of 1 × 3 plus 1 × 1 = 4; loop 3 is a right triangle with legs 2 and 3, area ½ × 2 × 3 = 3.
  4. So τ1 = τ2 > τ3.
Answer — C — τ1 = τ2 > τ3.
Common slip. Comparing perimeters, or assuming the L-shape must have less area than the square because it looks thinner. Count the squares.
13 of 40 APT · Physics 2026 paper, APT Physics Q3 mark done
Recognise it by: A capacitor in a DC loop passes current only while it charges

Consider the circuit shown. Initially the three-way switch is at position 2. After some time the switch is moved to position 3.

Which of the following describes the behaviour of the LED when the switch is moved from position 2 to 3?

  1. The LED glows as long as the switch is at position 3.
  2. The LED glows for a short interval of time.
  3. The LED does not glow.
  4. (Information provided is insufficient.)

How to see it

Ask what is in the loop once the switch moves. If the only source is a charged capacitor, the current is a decaying pulse.

Working

  1. At position 2 the capacitor is across the battery and charges up. The LED branch is not in that loop.
  2. Moving to position 3 connects the charged capacitor through the resistor and the LED.
  3. The capacitor discharges: the current starts at V0/R and decays as e−t/RC. There is no source of steady emf in this loop.
  4. So the LED flashes and dies away — it glows for a short interval, of order RC.
Answer — B — the LED glows for a short interval of time.
Common slip. Answering A because the switch stays at 3. A closed circuit is not enough; sustained current needs a sustained emf, and a capacitor supplies charge only once.
14 of 40 APT · Physics 2026 paper, APT Physics Q4 mark done
Recognise it by: Same N, same A, different length ⇒ different L

Two solenoids, P and Q, have the same number of turns. In solenoid P the wire is tightly wound; in Q the windings are equally spaced with a gap equal to the radius of the wire. Both have the same core material and the same area of cross section.

If the same current is passed through both, find the ratio of the energy stored in P to that in Q.

  1. 1 : 2
  2. 1 : 1
  3. 3 : 2
  4. 2 : 1

How to see it

Energy is ½LI² with the same I, so the whole question is the ratio of the two inductances — and the only thing that differs is the length.

Working

  1. Let the wire have radius r, so its diameter is 2r.
  2. P (touching turns): pitch = 2r, so lP = 2Nr.
  3. Q (gap of r between turns): pitch = 2r + r = 3r, so lQ = 3Nr.
  4. L = μ0N²A/l, so L ∝ 1/l when N and A are fixed.
  5. U = ½LI² ⇒ UP : UQ = lQ : lP = 3 : 2.
Answer — C — 3 : 2.
Common slip. Taking the gap as a whole wire diameter, which gives 4Nr and the ratio 2 : 1 (option D). The gap is one radius.
15 of 40 APT · Physics 2026 paper, APT Physics Q5 mark done
Recognise it by: Springs either side of a block act in parallel

A block of mass m oscillates with frequency f1 on spring P (constant k1) alone, and with f2 on spring Q (constant k2) alone. The block is now placed on a frictionless horizontal plane and connected to both springs, as shown.

What is the frequency with which the block oscillates when displaced a distance X from its mean position O?

The four options as the paper prints them:

How to see it

Displace the block and ask which way each spring pushes. If both push it back, they add.

Working

  1. Move the block right by x: spring P stretches and pulls it left by k1x; spring Q compresses and pushes it left by k2x.
  2. Both restore, so they act in parallel: keff = k1 + k2.
  3. fnet = (1/2π)√((k1 + k2)/m).
  4. Now express it through the given frequencies: f1² = k1/(4π²m), f2² = k2/(4π²m), so fnet² = f1² + f2².
  5. Option B is the same physics but drops the 1/2π, so it is dimensionally an angular frequency, not a frequency. Option D is exact.
Answer — D — fnet = √(f1² + f2²).
Common slip. Calling the two springs “in series” because they are on opposite sides, and using the reduced constant k1k2/(k1 + k2) — option C. Series means the same force through both; here they share the displacement, not the force.

Recognise it by: Lens first, then treat its image as the mirror's object

A convex lens of focal length 4 cm and a convex mirror of radius of curvature 4 cm are placed 12 cm apart as shown. The image formed by the lens has a magnification of −1.

At what distance behind the mirror is the image formed?

  1. 4·00 cm
  2. 2·66 cm
  3. 2·00 cm
  4. 1·33 cm

How to see it

m = −1 for a lens is a standard configuration: object and image both at 2f. That is the only thing you need from the first stage.

Working

  1. Lens: m = −1 means the object is at 2f = 8 cm and the image forms at 2f = 8 cm on the far side.
  2. The mirror is 12 cm from the lens, so that image lies 12 − 8 = 4 cm in front of the mirror and becomes the mirror's object: u = −4 cm.
  3. Convex mirror: f = +R/2 = +2 cm.
  4. 1/v + 1/u = 1/f ⇒ 1/v = ½ − (−¼) = ½ + ¼ = 3/4.
  5. v = 4/3 = 1·33 cm, positive, i.e. behind the mirror — virtual, as a convex mirror always gives.
Answer — D — 1·33 cm behind the mirror.
Common slip. Using f = 4 cm for the mirror. The 4 cm is the radius; the focal length is 2 cm. Using 4 cm gives 2 cm, which is option C.
17 of 40 APT · Physics 2026 paper, APT Physics Q7 mark done
Recognise it by: Null point of two like charges lies between them

Two positive point charges Q1 and Q2 are at fixed positions along a line, with Q2 > Q1.

In which of the regions R, S or T along this line can a positive charge Q3 be placed so that the net electric force acting on it is zero?

  1. only in region R
  2. only in region S
  3. either in region R or S
  4. either in region S or T

How to see it

Two forces cancel only if they point in opposite directions. Sketch the two arrows in each region before doing any algebra.

Working

  1. Both source charges are positive, so each repels Q3.
  2. In R (left of both): Q1 pushes left and Q2 pushes left. Same direction — they can never cancel.
  3. In T (right of both): both push right. Same again.
  4. In S (between them): Q1 pushes right, Q2 pushes left. Opposite, so a null point exists.
  5. It is unique: moving from Q1 towards Q2, Q1's push falls and Q2's rises, crossing exactly once — nearer Q1, since Q2 is the larger charge.
Answer — B — only in region S.
Common slip. Reasoning from the sizes of the charges instead of from the directions. Q2 > Q1 only tells you where in S the null point lies, not whether one exists outside.
18 of 40 APT · Physics 2026 paper, APT Physics Q8 mark done
Recognise it by: Thermal expansion: convert αv to αl, then add both blocks

The arrangement shown consists of two metal blocks at room temperature, one of silver (Ag) and one of nickel (Ni), fixed to rigid supports. The distance between the supports stays at 601 mm. Each block has a side length of 300 mm.

What temperature increase is required for both blocks to completely fill the gap, assuming uniform thermal expansion?

(Given: coefficient of volumetric expansion of silver (αv)Ag = 54 × 10−6 K−1 and of nickel (αv)Ni = 39 × 10−6 K−1.)

  1. 36 K
  2. 54 K
  3. 108 K
  4. (Cannot determine the temperature difference, without knowing the initial temperature of the blocks.)

How to see it

The gap closes along one direction only, so you need linear coefficients; the data is volumetric.

Working

  1. Gap = 601 − (300 + 300) = 1 mm.
  2. αl = αv/3: silver 18 × 10−6, nickel 13 × 10−6 K−1.
  3. Both blocks grow towards the gap: Δl = (300)(18 × 10−6)ΔT + (300)(13 × 10−6)ΔT
  4. = 300 × 31 × 10−6 ΔT = 9·3 × 10−3 ΔT mm.
  5. Set equal to 1 mm: ΔT = 1/(9·3 × 10−3) = 107·5 ≈ 108 K.
  6. D is wrong because expansion depends on the change in temperature, not on where it starts.
Answer — C — about 108 K.
Common slip. Using αv directly. That would triple every expansion and give roughly 36 K — which is option A, put there for exactly this mistake.

Recognise it by: Bohr angular momentum nh/2π does not depend on Z

What is the ratio of the angular momentum of an electron in the nth shell of a Li+2 atom to the angular momentum of an electron in the (n+1)th shell of a hydrogen atom?

  1. n : (n+1)
  2. (n+1) : 1
  3. n : 3(n+1)
  4. 3n : (n+1)

How to see it

Write the Bohr quantisation condition and check which symbols actually appear in it.

Working

  1. Bohr's second postulate: L = nh/2π.
  2. The atomic number Z appears in the radius (∝ n²/Z), in the energy (∝ Z²/n²) and in the speed (∝ Z/n) — but not in the angular momentum.
  3. Li+2 is hydrogen-like (one electron, Z = 3), so its nth shell still has L = nh/2π.
  4. Hydrogen's (n+1)th shell: L = (n+1)h/2π.
  5. Ratio = n : (n+1).
Answer — A — n : (n+1).
Common slip. Slipping a factor of Z = 3 in, giving option C or D. Options C and D exist solely to catch that.
20 of 40 APT · Physics 2026 paper, APT Physics Q10 mark done
Recognise it by: Calorimetry: more heat capacity in the hot body ⇒ hotter mixture

Three different metal samples X, Y and Z, each of mass 75 g, were heated to 120°C and then immersed in separate identical beakers containing 100 g of water at 25°C.

If the specific heat capacities satisfy cX > cY > cZ, which substance will show a higher equilibrium temperature?

(Assume no heat is lost to the surroundings and the specific heat capacity of the beakers is negligible.)

  1. X
  2. Y
  3. Z
  4. (All will show the same equilibrium temperature.)

How to see it

Write the mixing temperature as a weighted average and see which way the weight moves it.

Working

  1. Heat lost = heat gained: mc(120 − T) = mwcw(T − 25).
  2. Rearranged, T = (mc·120 + mwcw·25) / (mc + mwcw) — a weighted average of 120°C and 25°C.
  3. The weights are the two heat capacities. The masses are the same in all three experiments, so the metal's weight mc rises with c.
  4. The larger c is, the more the average is pulled towards 120°C.
  5. cX is the largest, so X gives the highest equilibrium temperature.
Answer — A — X.
Common slip. Reasoning that a high specific heat means the metal “holds on to” its heat and therefore releases less. It holds more heat per degree, so it delivers more as it cools.
21 of 40 APT · Physics 2025 paper, APT Physics Q1 mark done
Recognise it by: Superpose two fields; a shell screens only its own charge

A point charge +Q is near a thin non-conducting shell of radius L carrying an equal charge +Q uniformly distributed on its surface.

Point 1 is midway on the line joining +Q and the centre of the shell; point 2 is inside the shell at a distance L/2 from the centre.

Choose the option that correctly describes the total electric field at points 1 and 2.

  1. The electric field is zero at point 1 but is non-zero at point 2.
  2. The electric field is non-zero at point 1 but is zero at point 2.
  3. The electric field is non-zero at both points 1 and 2.
  4. The electric field is zero at both points 1 and 2.

How to see it

Two separate results: a uniformly charged shell looks like a point charge from outside and contributes nothing inside — but that is only its own field.

Working

  1. Point 1. It is 2L from +Q and 2L from the centre of the shell. From outside, the shell acts as a point charge +Q at its centre.
  2. So the two contributions are both kQ/(2L)², and they point in opposite directions (each away from its own positive charge). They cancel: the field at point 1 is zero.
  3. Point 2. Inside the shell, the shell's own field is zero — that is the shell theorem.
  4. But the external point charge +Q still produces a field there, and the shell is non-conducting, so no charge rearranges to cancel it. Nothing screens it.
  5. Total field at point 2 is therefore not zero.
Answer — The physics gives A — zero at 1, non-zero at 2. SNU's key says D.
Common slip. Remembering “the field inside a shell is zero” without the words that matter: zero due to the shell's own charge. Any outside charge is still felt inside a non-conducting shell.
Careful — the paper itself. SNU's key gives D (zero at both). That is the answer for a conducting shell, where induced charge does screen the interior — and the question says non-conducting, which is the one word the whole question turns on. Work it as A; the word ‘non-conducting’ in an exam is always the signal that screening is off.

Recognise it by: Read a T–V diagram: horizontal = isothermal, vertical = isochoric

A reversible cyclic process is carried out on one mole of an ideal monatomic gas. The T–V diagram is shown, with the processes labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4.

Which of these statements are true?

P — Processes 1 and 3 occur at constant pressure.
Q — The gas absorbs heat energy from the surroundings in process 2.
R — In process 4, the work done on the gas by the surroundings is equal to the heat energy released by the gas.

  1. Only P and Q
  2. Only P and R
  3. Only Q and R
  4. All P, Q, and R

How to see it

On a T–V plot an isobaric process is a straight line through the origin, because PV = nRT makes T ∝ V at fixed P.

Working

  1. P. Processes 1 and 3 run up and down the diagram at essentially fixed V, and neither is a straight line through the origin. They are isochoric, not isobaric. False.
  2. Q. Process 2 is horizontal: T constant while V increases — isothermal expansion. ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, so Q = W, and W done by the gas is positive. The gas absorbs heat. True.
  3. R. Process 4 is the isothermal compression. Again ΔU = 0, so the work done on the gas equals the heat it releases. True.
  4. Only Q and R.
Answer — C — only Q and R.
Common slip. Reading a horizontal line on a T–V plot as “constant pressure” out of habit from P–V diagrams. Always check which quantities the axes carry.

Recognise it by: Same rod, same material ⇒ heat flow ∝ ΔT

Four cylindrical rods are made of the same material and have identical dimensions. The temperatures at each end are shown.

Which option correctly represents the rate of heat flow in the rods?

(Q is the symbol for heat flow; consider no heat is lost to the surroundings.)

  1. ΔQ1 > ΔQ3 = ΔQ2 > ΔQ4
  2. ΔQ4 > ΔQ2 > ΔQ3 > ΔQ1
  3. ΔQ2 > ΔQ3 > ΔQ4 = ΔQ1
  4. ΔQ4 > ΔQ2 > ΔQ1 = ΔQ3

How to see it

Conduction depends on the temperature difference, never on how hot the rod is.

Working

  1. dQ/dt = kAΔT/L, and k, A, L are the same for all four. So rank by ΔT alone.
  2. Rod 1: 30 − (−20) = 50 K.
  3. Rod 2: 80 − 10 = 70 K.
  4. Rod 3: 30 − (−5) = 35 K.
  5. Rod 4: 250 − 200 = 50 K.
  6. So ΔQ2 > ΔQ1 = ΔQ4 > ΔQ3.
  7. Option C is the only one that gets the two key facts right — rod 2 the largest, rods 1 and 4 equal.
Answer — C — rod 2 largest, rods 1 and 4 equal, rod 3 least.
Common slip. Ranking rod 4 first because 200°C and 250°C are the biggest numbers on the page. Its difference is only 50 K, the same as rod 1's.
Careful — the paper itself. Option C as printed reads ΔQ2 > ΔQ3 > ΔQ4 = ΔQ1, which puts rod 3 (35 K) above rods 1 and 4 (50 K). No option states the correct order; C is the key's answer and the only one with rod 2 largest and rods 1 and 4 equal, so its middle term is a misprint.

Recognise it by: Constant acceleration: v–t straight, a–t flat and non-zero

Which of the graphs given below represent/s the motion of an object with a constant, non-zero acceleration?

  1. Only V
  2. Only II and V
  3. Only III and V
  4. Only I, II and IV

How to see it

Identify what each axis carries, then ask what constant acceleration looks like on that pair of axes.

Working

  1. I — position against time, a straight line. Constant velocity, so a = 0. Constant acceleration would need a parabola.
  2. II — velocity against time, straight line with non-zero slope. Slope = acceleration = constant and non-zero. ✓
  3. III — velocity constant, so a = 0. Fails “non-zero”.
  4. IV — acceleration rising linearly, so it is not constant.
  5. V — acceleration constant and above the axis. ✓
Answer — B — only II and V.
Common slip. Including III. A flat line on a velocity graph is constant velocity; a flat line on an acceleration graph is constant acceleration. Same shape, different meaning.

Recognise it by: F = GMm/r² uses mass, not density

Planets X and Y have identical mass, but the density of planet Y is less than the density of planet X.

At which point is the rocket LIKELY to experience EQUAL magnitude of gravitational forces due to planets X and Y? (Point Q is the midpoint of the line joining the centres of the planets.)

  1. At point P, because planet X has a greater density.
  2. At point R, because planet Y is bigger.
  3. At point Q because the planets have the same mass.
  4. (Cannot determine without knowing the actual mass of both the planets.)

How to see it

Density changes the size of a planet, not the field it produces outside itself.

Working

  1. Outside a spherically symmetric body the field is GM/r² — it depends only on the total mass and the distance from the centre.
  2. The masses are equal, so the two pulls are equal exactly where the distances are equal: at the midpoint Q.
  3. Y is bigger only because it is less dense; that changes where its surface is, not its external field.
  4. D is wrong: the answer needs only that the masses are equal, not their value.
Answer — C — at point Q, because the planets have the same mass.
Common slip. Letting the drawing decide. Y is drawn much larger, which tempts you towards R, but size is irrelevant once you are outside both bodies.

Recognise it by: Same spring, different mass: T = 2π√(m/k)

A student attaches each of three frictionless carts P, Q and R in turn to a spring of constant k and displaces it. The position–time graphs for the three carts, over the same time window, are shown.

Based on the graphs, which option shows the correct relation between the masses of the carts?

  1. 2MP = MQ = MR
  2. MP = 2MQ = MR
  3. MP = 4MQ = MR
  4. MP = MQ = MR

How to see it

Count cycles in the same window — that gives the period — and remember mass goes as the square of the period.

Working

  1. Over the same window: P shows about 8 cycles, Q about 4, R about 8.
  2. So TP = TR and TQ = 2TP.
  3. T = 2π√(m/k) with the same k, so m ∝ T².
  4. MP = MR, and MQ = 4MP.
  5. Amplitude differs between the graphs and is a red herring — the period of SHM does not depend on amplitude.
Answer — C — the key's answer; the graphs give MQ = 4MP = 4MR.
Common slip. Using m ∝ T instead of T², which would make the factor 2 rather than 4.
Careful — the paper itself. Option C is printed as MP = 4MQ = MR, i.e. with Q as the lightest cart — but Q is the one oscillating slowest, so it must be the heaviest. C is still the key's answer and the only option carrying both MP = MR and a factor of 4; the factor is on the wrong side of the equals sign.

Recognise it by: Work–energy theorem: work done = change in kinetic energy

Shown below is a velocity–time graph for a box on a straight horizontal path under a single intermittent force from an external agent.

Which option correctly compares the work done on the box by the external agent during the intervals P, Q, R and S?

  1. WR > WP = WQ = WS
  2. WP > WS > WQ > WR
  3. WP = WS < WQ, WQ > WR
  4. WP = WS > WQ, WQ < WR

How to see it

Never integrate the force. Read the speed at each end of an interval and use ½mv².

Working

  1. P (0–20 s): v = 3 m/s throughout. ΔKE = 0, so WP = 0.
  2. Q (20–40 s): v goes from +3 to −3. Speed is 3 at both ends, so KE is unchanged and WQ = 0.
  3. R (40–60 s): v goes from −3 to +1. KE falls from 4·5m to 0·5m, so WR = −4m joules — the only non-zero one.
  4. S (60–80 s): v = 1 m/s throughout, WS = 0.
  5. So R is the only interval in which the agent does any work at all, and WP = WQ = WS = 0.
Answer — A — R stands apart, and P, Q and S are all equal.
Common slip. Thinking a reversal of direction must cost work. In Q the box turns right round and the net work is still zero, because the speed is the same at both ends.
Careful — the paper itself. Read as a signed comparison, option A is back to front: WR is −4m, which is less than the three zeros, not greater. A is the key's answer and the only option that gets WP = WQ = WS; it works if you read it as comparing magnitudes of work done.
28 of 40 APT · Physics 2025 paper, APT Physics Q8 mark done
Recognise it by: Which prism wins the tug-of-war on the colours?

A combination of red and blue light is incident on side 1 of a two-prism setup. After refraction through prism Q, the blue light exits from side 2 above the red light.

Which of the options given are correct concerning the refractive index of the material of prism Q?

  1. less than the refractive index of prism P as the light is dispersed more in prism P
  2. less than the refractive index of prism P as the light is dispersed less in prism P
  3. more than the refractive index of prism P as the light is dispersed more in prism P
  4. more than the refractive index of prism P as the light is dispersed less in prism P

How to see it

The two prisms are inverted relative to each other, so they deviate in opposite senses. Whichever disperses more decides the order of the colours at the exit.

Working

  1. In prism P, blue is refracted more than red, so inside P the blue ray is bent further — it runs below the red.
  2. Prism Q is inverted, so it bends the rays back the other way, and again blue more than red.
  3. The light leaves with blue above red, so Q has not merely undone P's dispersion — it has overturned it.
  4. For Q's dispersion to beat P's, Q must be the more strongly refracting material: nQ > nP, the light having been dispersed less in P.
  5. Had the two indices been equal, the emergent beam would have been white again, with the colours recombined.
Answer — D — higher index in Q, because P disperses less.
Common slip. Deciding on the basis of which prism the light meets first. Order does not matter; the net dispersion is the difference between the two, so the winner is whichever prism disperses more.

Recognise it by: Energy = V × charge, and charge is the area under the pulse

A defibrillator provides a current pulse as shown. This pulse delivers 140 J of electrical energy to the heart.

Which of the options below gives the best estimate for the potential difference across the defibrillator plates?

  1. 1 V
  2. 10 V
  3. 1000 V
  4. 1400 V

How to see it

A rectangular current pulse makes the charge trivial: height × width.

Working

  1. Read the pulse off the graph: height about 14 A, width from about 5 ms to about 17 ms, so roughly 12 ms.
  2. Charge q = I t = 14 × 12 × 10−3 = 0·168 C.
  3. Energy E = qV ⇒ V = 140 / 0·168 ≈ 833 V.
  4. The options are orders of magnitude apart, so 833 V rounds to the 1000 V option.
  5. It is also the physically sensible answer: defibrillators run at hundreds to thousands of volts.
Answer — C — about 1000 V.
Common slip. Reading the time axis in seconds. Using 12 s instead of 12 ms would give about 0·8 V, which is option A — and a defibrillator that ran on a volt would be useless.

Recognise it by: Rayleigh criterion θ = 1·22λ/D, then s = Lθ

Pointillism creates images from closely spaced dots, typically about 2 mm in diameter. Standing close, one sees the individual dots; from further away they blend.

Give the best estimate of the minimum distance a person with 20/20 vision should stand from the painting in order to see the dots blend into one another.

(Assume the wavelength to be 550 nm, and the diameter of the pupil is 2 mm.)

  1. 5·9 m
  2. 2·5 m
  3. 1·8 m
  4. 0·25 m

How to see it

Two dots blend when their angular separation drops below the eye's resolving angle. So find that angle and convert to a distance.

Working

  1. Resolving angle of the eye: θ = 1·22λ/D = 1·22 × 550 × 10−9 / (2 × 10−3)
  2. θ = 3·36 × 10−4 rad.
  3. Two dots 2 mm apart subtend s/L at distance L. They stop being resolved when s/L ≤ θ.
  4. L = s/θ = 2 × 10−3 / (3·36 × 10−4) ≈ 5·9 m.
  5. Note which way the inequality runs: further away means smaller angular separation, so 5·9 m is the minimum distance for blending.
Answer — A — about 5·9 m.
Common slip. Dropping the 1·22, which gives about 7·3 m, or inverting the last step. Check the direction of the answer: standing closer must make the dots easier to separate, not harder.

  4. 9 : 1

Every Bohr quantity scales as a power of Z and n: energy as Z²/n², radius as n²/Z, speed as Z/n, angular momentum as n alone.

Working

  1. En = −13·6 Z²/n² eV.
  2. Li2+, n = 3: −13·6 × 9/9 = −13·6 eV.
  3. H, n = 1: −13·6 eV.
  4. Ratio 1 : 1 — the Z² and the n² cancel exactly.

  1. 1 : 2
  2. 1 : 1
  3. 4 : 1
  4. 2 : 1

A larger nucleus charge pulls the orbit in (divide by Z); a higher shell pushes it out as the square (multiply by n²).

  1. rn = 0·529 n²/Z Å.
  2. He+, n = 2: 0·529 × 4/2 = 2 × 0·529 Å.
  3. H, n = 1: 0·529 Å.
  4. Ratio 2 : 1.

Common slip. Using n/Z (giving 1 : 1) — that is how the angular momentum would go if it depended on Z, which it does not. The radius goes as n².

  2. 2 : 1

  4. 1 : 2√2

The same voltage gives kinetic energy qV, which differs because the charges differ. Contrast the 2027 paper, where the momenta were equal and so were the wavelengths.

  1. K = qV, p = √(2mK) = √(2mqV), λ = h/p.
  2. λp/λα = √(mαqα / mpqp) = √(4 × 2) = √8.

Recognise it by: vd = μE and E = V/L: track the field, not the voltage

A potential difference V across a copper wire of length L gives its electrons a drift velocity v. The wire is replaced by a copper wire of the same cross-section but twice the length, and the potential difference is doubled. The temperature is unchanged.

What is the new drift velocity?

  1. v/2
  2. v
  3. 2v
  4. 4v

How to see it

The slope of the 2027 drift-velocity graph was the mobility μ, fixed by the material and temperature. So only the electric field inside the wire matters.

Working

  1. vd = μE, and μ is unchanged (same metal, same temperature).
  2. E = V/L: new field = 2V/2L = V/L, the same as before.
  3. So the drift velocity is unchanged: v.
  4. Cross-check: resistance doubles and voltage doubles, so the current I = nAevd is the same, and with the same A and n so is vd.

Recognise it by: Given αV? Divide by 3 before using ΔL = LαΔT

Steel rails 12 m long are laid at 20 °C. The hottest the track will get is 50 °C. The coefficient of volume expansion of the steel is 3·6 × 10−5 K−1.

What is the least gap that must be left between neighbouring rails?

  1. 12·96 mm
  2. 8·64 mm
  3. 4·32 mm
  4. 1·44 mm

How to see it

This is the trap SNU set in both 2026 and 2027: the coefficient given is volumetric, and a length expands with the linear one, α = αV/3.

Working

  1. α = 3·6 × 10−5/3 = 1·2 × 10−5 K−1.
  2. ΔT = 50 − 20 = 30 K.
  3. ΔL = 12 m × 1·2 × 10−5 × 30 = 4·32 × 10−3 m = 4·32 mm.
  4. Each rail pushes half its growth into the gap at either end, and its neighbour pushes in the other half, so each gap must absorb one full rail's growth.
Answer — C — 4·32 mm.
Common slip. Using αV directly, which gives 12·96 mm, three times too big.
36 of 40 APT · Physics Predicted 2027, APT Physics V6 mark done
Recognise it by: Free expansion into vacuum: Q = 0, W = 0, so ΔU = 0 — yet entropy rises

An ideal gas in an insulated container is released through a valve into an evacuated chamber, also insulated. Which statement about the gas, once it settles, is correct?

  1. Its temperature falls, because it did work in expanding.
  2. Its temperature is unchanged and its entropy increases.
  3. Its temperature is unchanged and its entropy is unchanged.
  4. Its temperature rises, because its molecules speed up into the vacuum.

How to see it

Apply the first law to the whole process, then remember entropy is a state function: compute it along any reversible path between the same two states.

Working

  1. Insulated: Q = 0. Expanding against nothing: W = 0.
  2. ΔU = Q − W = 0, and an ideal gas's U depends only on T, so T is unchanged.
  3. Same end states as a reversible isothermal expansion, for which ΔS = nR ln(V2/V1) > 0.
  4. So the entropy increases — the process is irreversible; the gas never goes back by itself.
Answer — B — temperature unchanged, entropy increases.
Common slip. Reasoning ‘Q = 0 so ΔS = 0’. ΔS = ∫dQ/T holds only along a reversible path, and free expansion is not one.
37 of 40 APT · Physics Predicted 2027, APT Physics V7 mark done
Recognise it by: Lens-maker's formula uses the relative refractive index

Assertion (A): A biconvex glass lens (n = 1·5) placed in a liquid of refractive index 1·6 behaves as a diverging lens.

Reason (R): In the lens-maker's formula 1/f = (nrel − 1)(1/R1 − 1/R2), nrel is the refractive index of the lens relative to the surrounding medium.

  1. Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
  2. Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
  3. A is true but R is false.
  4. A is false but R is true.

How to see it

This is the flip side of the 2027 assertion–reason question: a lens's shape does not decide whether it converges; the lens compared with its surroundings does.

Working

  1. nrel = 1·5/1·6 < 1, so (nrel − 1) < 0.
  2. For a biconvex lens (1/R1 − 1/R2) > 0, so 1/f < 0: a diverging lens. A is true.
  3. R is the standard statement of the formula, true, and it is exactly what makes A happen.
Answer — A — both true, and R explains A.
Common slip. Reasoning from shape — ‘thick in the middle, so it converges’. That is only true when the lens is denser than what surrounds it.
38 of 40 APT · Physics Predicted 2027, APT Physics V8 mark done
Recognise it by: Line charge: E = λ/(2πε0r), radial; resolve with x/r

A long straight wire along the z-axis carries a uniform linear charge density λ. What is the x-component of the electric field at the point (4, 3, 0) m?

  1. λ/(10πε0)
  2. 3λ/(50πε0)
  3. λ/(8πε0)
  4. 2λ/(25πε0)

How to see it

Gauss's law gives the magnitude at perpendicular distance r from the wire. The field points radially away in the xy-plane, so its x-share is x/r.

Working

  1. Perpendicular distance from the z-axis: r = √(4² + 3²) = 5 m.
  2. |E| = λ/(2πε0 × 5) = λ/(10πε0).
  3. Ex = |E| × 4/5 = 4λ/(50πε0) = 2λ/(25πε0).
  4. (Ey = 3λ/(50πε0), and Ez = 0.)
Answer — D — 2λ/(25πε0).
Common slip. Using the x-coordinate as the distance (λ/(8πε0)), or stopping at the magnitude. The distance is to the wire; then resolve.
39 of 40 APT · Physics Predicted 2027, APT Physics V9 mark done
Recognise it by: r = mv/qB = √(2mK)/qB: write it in what is held equal

A proton, a deuteron and an alpha particle enter the same uniform magnetic field perpendicular to it, all with the same kinetic energy. How do the radii of their circular paths compare?

  1. rp < rd < rα
  2. rp = rα < rd
  3. rα < rp < rd
  4. rp = rd = rα

How to see it

The 2027 paper held the speed equal; here kinetic energy is equal, so momentum is √(2mK). Express r in m and q only.

Working

  1. r = √(2mK)/(qB) ∝ √m/q at fixed K and B.
  2. Proton (m = 1, q = 1): √1/1 = 1.
  3. Deuteron (m = 2, q = 1): √2 ≈ 1·41.
  4. Alpha (m = 4, q = 2): √4/2 = 1. So rp = rα < rd.
Answer — B — rp = rα < rd.
Common slip. Going by mass alone and putting the alpha particle largest. Its double charge exactly undoes its √4 = 2.
40 of 40 APT · Physics Predicted 2027, APT Physics V10 mark done
Recognise it by: RC: at t = 0 the capacitor is a wire; after a long time it is a break

An uncharged 10 μF capacitor is connected in series with a 100 kΩ resistor, a switch and an ideal 12 V battery. What is the current in the circuit just after the switch is closed, and a long time after?

  1. 0·12 mA and 0·12 mA
  2. 1·2 mA and 0
  3. 0 and 0·12 mA
  4. 0·12 mA and 0

How to see it

An empty capacitor has no voltage across it, so at first the whole battery drives the resistor. A full one carries the whole battery voltage, leaving none for the resistor.

Working

  1. At t = 0: VC = 0, so I = 12 V/100 kΩ = 1·2 × 10−4 A = 0·12 mA.
  2. As t → ∞: VC = 12 V, so VR = 0 and I = 0.
  3. Between, I = 0·12 e−t/RC mA with RC = 105 × 10−5 = 1 s.
  4. So 0·12 mA, then 0.
Answer — D — 0·12 mA and 0.
Common slip. Reversing the two limits (option C), or a power-of-ten slip with kΩ (1·2 mA). A capacitor in a DC loop passes current only while charging — the 2026 paper's lesson.

That is all of it

160 questions — every one SNU has released for the current pattern, and forty predicted variations on the types it favours.

Where to go next

  • The older four-section sample paper (60 questions plus an essay) and the 2012 paper are in Sample-Papers/. They are a different test — verbal reasoning and a typed essay, 120 minutes — but the reasoning and quantitative items are the same skills, and they are the only other genuine SNU material there is.
  • For the APT, the Physics and Maths collections elsewhere in this repository cover the syllabus several times over.
  • For SNU Chennai, the SNUCEE has no model papers at all — the university says so in print. Its aptitude half is the same kind of material as SNUSAT, so this deck is the nearest practice there is; the subject half needs the SNUCEE syllabus PDFs and your own board papers. Note that unlike SNUSAT, the SNUCEE does have negative marking.

Full provenance for every paper is in the README beside this file.
